paragraphs.heading: Fungi that live as single cells
paragraphs.text: A yeast is a fungus that lives mostly as single cells and multiplies by budding or by fission, splitting in two. Yeasts are eukaryotic microbes that arose hundreds of millions of years ago. At least 1,500 species are known, about 1% of all described fungi. A typical yeast cell is 3–4 μm across, though some grow to 40 μm. Their single-celled habit sets them apart from molds, which grow hyphae.

paragraphs.heading: Budding and beyond
paragraphs.text: Most yeasts reproduce without sex by mitosis, and many do it by budding, a cell division that produces unequal parts. Some species can form strings of linked budding cells, called pseudohyphae or false hyphae, and so take on features of many-celled life. Dimorphic fungi are species that can take either the yeast form or the mold form, switching with temperature or other conditions.

paragraphs.heading: Bread, beer and the lab
paragraphs.text: The yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae turns carbohydrates into carbon dioxide and alcohols through fermentation. People have used what it makes in baking and in brewing alcoholic drinks for thousands of years. The same species is now a key model organism in cell biology and one of the most thoroughly studied eukaryotic microbes. Researchers grow it to learn in detail how eukaryotic cells work, and through them human biology.

paragraphs.heading: What yeasts live on
paragraphs.text: Yeasts draw their energy from organic compounds and need no sunlight to grow. Most of their carbon comes from hexose sugars, for example glucose and fructose, or from sucrose and maltose, and some can also use ribose, alcohols and organic acids. Some yeasts must have oxygen; others can manage without it but can also use it. Unlike bacteria, no known yeast lives only without oxygen. Most grow best when conditions are neutral or slightly acidic.

paragraphs.heading: An ancient helper
paragraphs.text: Yeasts are probably among the earliest organisms people domesticated. In Egyptian ruins, archaeologists found grinding stones and baking chambers for yeast-raised bread, along with drawings of bakeries and breweries 4,000 years old. In Israel, vessels thought to have held beer and mead, from about 5,000, 3,000 and 2,500 years ago, still held yeast colonies that had survived. These gave the first direct biological evidence that early cultures used yeast.

paragraphs.heading: Proving yeast is alive
paragraphs.text: Anton van Leeuwenhoek first saw yeast under a microscope in 1680, but he did not take it for a living thing. Theodor Schwann recognized yeasts as fungi in 1837. In 1857 Louis Pasteur found that bubbling oxygen through yeast broth boosted growth but held back fermentation, which was later called the Pasteur effect. He also proved that living yeasts, not a chemical catalyst, carry out alcoholic fermentation.

paragraphs.heading: Not one family
paragraphs.text: Some yeasts, such as Candida albicans, are opportunistic pathogens that can infect people. Others have lately been put to work making electricity in microbial fuel cells and ethanol for biofuel. Although the word yeast is often treated as another name for Saccharomyces cerevisiae, yeasts do not form a single natural group. They turn up in two separate phyla, the Ascomycota and the Basidiomycota.
